title: Theatre review: The Cherry Orchard with Kristin Scott Thomas & Stephen Mangan
transcript: Hello and welcome to Theatre Reviews with Paul Seven. I'm here at the Harold Pinter Theatre to see Kristin Scott Thomas and Stephen Mangan in The Cherry Orchard. >> >> Every production of The Cherry Orchard is different. Like life, it's so open to interpretation. But there's always a sense of doom. And there's always a comical bubble of illusions shielding those who are looking doom in the face. So what makes this production at the Harold Pinter Theatre special? Well, this is a particularly star-studded production. Uh not only Kristin Scott Thomas and Stephen Mangan starring, but top playwright Conor McPherson um providing a reimagining and Ian Rickson directing. But it's also blessed with a cast of the highest quality. Keep watching and I'll tell you lots more about The Cherry Orchard. But first, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. And visit my website theatre.reviews, where you'll find not only my reviews, but my roundups of other critics' reviews, including of The Cherry Orchard. Conor McPherson's language is blunt and speaks to a modern audience. Chloe Lamford's decaying, damp-looking set and Sussy Owusu-Walden's costumes, which mix period and modern elements, all give the production a sense of time passing. The mixed bunch of characters are either living in the past or seeking to preserve it. The theme of resistance to change is timeless. The specific change in this case is the old Russian hierarchy round about the turn from the 19th to 20th century. Uh it's crumbling uh in the face of the rising middle class. Lyubov, played magnificently by Kristin Scott Thomas, is the matriarch of a grand house and estate um the destitute successor to uh her previously rich and powerful forefathers. This estate includes, of course, the cherry orchard. It's a cute touch in this production for the characters to look out onto us, the audience, when referring to the orchard. We are, it seems, both the past, condemned to perish, uh and the future that they will never see. Kristin Scott Thomas is all at sea, a rudderless ship, fiddling with her hair, um offering rictus smiles, uh distractedly hugging people in a half-hearted uh attempt to cure their sadness. Looking vacantly as if seeing the past or a different reality. Sentences trailing off. She continues to behave like the lady of the manor, giving away money she doesn't have, while the debts pile up. And always looking to take flight to Paris to join her unfaithful lover, preferring to keep the memory of the estate's past rather grapple with the modern-day challenges. Through the next 2 and 1/2 hours, the people around her interact like a chamber orchestra, uh sometimes in harmony, sometimes in conflict, fast, slow, sniping, soothing, and all the while revealing more and more of their characters and their illusions and their vulnerabilities. So many of the characters are lost in their illusions, unable to articulate their thoughts or even finish their sentences in the face of the reality before them. Luba's brother, Leo, is so inflated in his self-importance, but is actually a total scrounger and very unpleasant. He could be a template for a certain ex-royal of today. Always reassuring himself and those around him that something will turn up. Peter White gives him just the right mix of nasty and pathetic. Jeff Rawle brings more pathos to Boris, an impoverished landowner, smiling, but always desperate to borrow some money. Jack Riddiford is the perpetual student Petya, even at 30 years old, still talking of graduation. He speaks of revolution, but needs the aristocracy to revolt against. Like Luba, the other women also look to feckless men for salvation. Their love, repeatedly unreciprocated. Anastasia Martin is Luba's unstable daughter. Viniette Robinson gives a powerful performance as the adopted daughter, Varya, tight-laced, trying to manage the finances, but wishes she just could get out of there and be a nun. Megan Cusack is the servant Dunyasha, taking advantage of the breakdown of the class system to dress up and flirt with well, got to be the attractive man. Saddest and funniest of all, Karl Johnson plays Firs, the old retainer, literally living in the past because of his dementia, but coming up with golden lines like, "You're wearing the wrong trousers." Now, Karl Johnson is an actor I've seen many times on stage, and he never disappoints. Only Yermolai looks to the future. He's from peasant stock and well aware of his apparent inferiority. Uh "Sorry" is his most used word, and a wide-eyed nervous laugh is never far away. But, he's part of a new generation of self-made rich men. He's been in love with Lyuba since childhood. But, he sees the future that the estate must be commercialized to survive, that the cherry orchard must go. But, his illusion is that saving the estate will win over Lyuba. His belief in money as the way to his ideal is as deluded as the head-in-the-sand attitude of those around him. And he's blind to the possibility of happiness with Varya. Stephen Mangan is wonderful in this role, giving a light comic vulnerability to a character that can seem in some productions unpleasantly cruel. This production of The Cherry Orchard is a masterful reimagining from Conor McPherson uh that is brought to life by perfect cast and Ian Rickson's impeccable direction. I give The Cherry Orchard four stars. >> >> I hope you found this review interesting and useful. And if you did, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel, and you'll be the first to know about my future reviews. Uh you can read my reviews and my roundups of other critics' reviews at theatre.reviews, and you can follow me on Threads, uh Mastodon, Blue Sky, and Instagram. Happy theatergoing.
